title: The Great Birdie Copycat
spine: A cozy window-side game of copying birds escalates into a wild, crumb-filled romp until we must decide how to keep our new feathered friends happy.

window_spot.role: The cozy place where we watch the birds
window_spot.default: the kitchen window with the feeder stuck right to the glass

copycat_move.role: The silly way we try to move like a bird
copycat_move.default: flap our arms fast like a chickadee

segments.text: We are snuggled on the couch by {window_spot}. Tap, tap, tap! A bold little sparrow hops right up to the glass. It pecks the window and stares at us with one shiny eye. “Chirp!” we say. The sparrow tilts its head. “Chirp, chirp!” it says right back! We flap our arms fast. {copycat_move}. The sparrow flaps too! The game of copycat begins.

“Hop like birdies!” we say. We hop low. Hop, hop! We hop higher. Hop, hop, hop! We hop SO high — bonk! Our heads bump the bottom of the table. Soft bonk! The sparrow just keeps hopping on the sill. Hop, hop, hop. Like nothing happened. Then — zoom! A tiny chickadee swoops in. It grabs a seed. Zoom! Away it goes. Zoom in, grab, zoom away! “Chirp!” says the sparrow. “Chirp, chirp!” we say back.

“Flap like birdies!” we say. We flap our arms fast. Flap, flap! We flap faster. Flapflapflapflap! Oh no — wobble, wobble — plop! We tumble onto the couch cushions in a giggly heap. We still can’t fly! The sparrow stares with one shiny eye. Then — flap, flap! A tiny chickadee swoops in. It grabs a seed. Flap, flap — away it goes! Showing off how it’s done. “Chirp!” says the sparrow. “Chirp, chirp!” we giggle back.

We are puffed and giggly from all that copying. "What did you find?" we ask the sparrow. It just chirps. So we put out one little crumb. The sparrow comes! Then a whole handful — five birds come! Then we dump out the WHOLE bag. Flap, flap, flap! Birds everywhere! Hopping on the rail. Perching on the chair. "Chirp!" "Chirp, chirp!" The porch is a birdie traffic jam. And through it all, the sparrow hops back to the window, right beside our hands on the glass, and stays.

A big round pigeon lands on the feeder. Thump! Too big! Seeds spill everywhere. "I fixed it!" he seems to say. All the birds eat off the floor. But wait! The little birds get pushed aside. We sprinkle extra seeds in a special spot just for them. The sparrow chirps. "Chirp!" we say back. "Chirp, chirp!" We watch the sparrow take one seed, slow, and settle its feathers down flat.

A big round pigeon lands on the feeder. Thump! Too big! Seeds spill everywhere. "I fixed it!" he seems to say. All the birds eat off the floor. But look! The mama bird stuffs her beak and zooms off. We follow her with our eyes. A tiny nest! Three fuzzy heads! We put out a special pile just for her. She zooms back and forth, back and forth. We stay at the window and watch her go.

choice_points.question: "Well?" the sparrow seems to say with its shiny eye. "How should we play? Should we hop like birdies, or flap like birdies?"
"Oh no!" the sparrow chirps, looking at the spilled seeds and the busy mama bird. "What should we do now? Should we share the seeds with the little birds, or find out where the mama bird is going?"

iterations.why: The story is full of motion and sound but the birds are treated as entertainment; the child and the sparrow never quite look at each other with fondness, so the ending lands on the mess rather than on the company.
editor_notes: In s1, the sparrow 'stares at us with one shiny eye' — give the child one small act of noticing back: a quiet line where the child sees something specific about the sparrow (a ruffled feather, a quick blink) before the game starts.

In s2a and s2b, the child copies the bird but the bird never copies the child in a way that feels like being seen; let the sparrow do one small, deliberate imitation of the child (a head tilt, a hop pattern) so the game becomes mutual rather than one-sided.

In s3, 'The porch is a birdie traffic jam' is funny but the sparrow gets lost in the crowd; end the segment with the sparrow coming back to the window or the child's hand, so the original companion is not swallowed by the spectacle.

In s4a, 'our hearts full and happy' tells the feeling instead of paying it as attention; replace it with a watched detail — the sparrow eating one seed slowly, or settling its feathers — so the warmth is shown, not declared.

In s4b, 'We helped a whole birdie family' is a conclusion about helpfulness; let the moment stay with the mama bird and the child watching her go, so the tenderness is in the staying, not the summary.

iterations.why: The story already pairs a lively, mouth-pleasing copycat game with a quiet ending in which the sparrow simply stays beside the child's hands on the glass — companionship paid as attention, exactly what a bedtime read-aloud needs.
